title: Beyond Immune Classification: A Root-Driver and Systemic Barrier Framework for Allergic and Autoimmune Diseases
content: Background: Allergic and autoimmune diseases are clinically heterogeneous and impose substantial health burdens. Although disease-specific immunotherapies have produced important advances, incomplete understanding of disease initiation, heterogeneous treatment responses, persistent comorbidity, and limited prevention options motivate investigation of potentially modifiable upstream contributors.Hypothesis: Integrative Orthomolecular Systems Medicine (I-OM) proposes that a subset of seemingly disparate immune-mediated disorders may be influenced by overlapping dietary, metabolic, nutritional, infectious, environmental, endocrine, developmental, and other contributors. These influences may converge partly on dysfunction of epithelial and other physiological barriers, microbial ecosystems, and host repair processes. We designate the proposed network-level convergence construct Systemic Leaky Barrier Syndrome (SLBS), extending an earlier conceptual preprint; SLBS is not an established diagnostic syndrome or a proven common cause.Framework: We specify ten I-OM root-driver domains and a four-step reasoning workflow—Divide, Examine, Reconnect, Intervene—while differentiating established disease-specific interventions, generally appropriate correction of documented abnormalities, and experimental adjuncts. Candidate interventions include individualized dietary quality and metabolic strategies, correction of deficiencies, investigation of confirmed infectious or dental sources, avoidance of hazardous exposures, endocrine care when indicated, and selected investigational nutritional or immune-regulatory approaches.Testing: The model predicts that prospectively defined multisite barrier signatures and actionable upstream contributors will stratify some patient subgroups and that a standardized I-OM assessment pathway may improve outcomes beyond an attention-matched, guideline-concordant comparator. These predictions must be tested with validated measurements, disease-specific endpoints, transparent harms reporting, and independently replicated trials.Conclusion: The scientific contribution of I-OM is not a claim of demonstrated cure or a replacement for immunology, but a falsifiable, safety-conscious approach to linking upstream investigation, multisystem biology, and clinical outcomes.
